prologue: From the journal of John H. Watson, M.D.

London, the first week of January, 1891. The snow has come and gone, and left the streets the colour of old pewter. My friend Sherlock Holmes has been out at odd hours for a week, and in at odder ones, and when I call at Baker Street he is either sitting in a cloud of blue smoke with his eyes shut, or standing at the window looking at nothing, with his fingers drumming on the sill.

He has told me nothing, which is in itself a kind of news. In ten years I have learned that Holmes is silent only when a matter is very large, or very dangerous, or both. I did not know, then, how large. I did not know that in the autumn of that year the whole world would believe him dead.

What follows is the account of the months between, as nearly as it can be set down. The choices were his. I have only the right to say that, whichever way he went, I should have gone with him if I had been asked.

howToPlay.heading: Your Part
howToPlay.body: The Case-Book on your table holds five volumes. The thick one is the major case, The Final Problem of 1891. The four thin ones are minor cases that stand alone: The Speckled Band (1883), A Scandal in Bohemia (1888), The Blue Carbuncle (1889) and The Red-Headed League (1890). A minor case is four scenes long, shares nothing with the major case, and is a good way to learn the game. The shelf remembers which endings you have found, and offers to resume an unfinished case. The rest of this page is about The Final Problem. You are Sherlock Holmes, from the first week of January 1891, hunting a man who has never been charged with a crime. Each scene is a dated report. You read it, and choose how to answer. Tap an option once to mark it, and again to confirm it. What you choose changes what comes next, and some doors open only for a detective who has done the right things earlier. You choose your road early, within a few scenes.

howToPlay.heading: Evidence, Standing and Nerve
howToPlay.body: Three gauges run from minus ten to plus ten. Evidence is what you can prove in a court. Standing is the trust of Scotland Yard, the magistrates and the press. Nerve is your own health and calm. When a gauge falls to minus seven, a warning card appears. At minus ten, the story ends in ruin. Watch the lowest gauge more than the highest.

howToPlay.heading: The Strand
howToPlay.body: Under the three gauges run three smaller lines, which the game calls the Strand, after the street and the magazine. Hours is time in hand: slow, patient work spends it. Hands is the people at your disposal: Watson, the boys, the Yard's men. Wires is your reach: a telegram, a file, an informant, the press. Each line runs from minus eight to plus eight, and has its own warning card at minus five. Any one of them at minus eight cuts the Strand, and the Professor goes untouched. A Strand line that is short also makes a gauge harder to fill. Keep the three in step, and do not spend the same line twice. Watson notices when one runs short, and says so in his notebook.

howToPlay.heading: Gambits
howToPlay.body: Some choices are a gamble, and show a percentage. The odds rise or fall with a gauge named in the scene. A gauge that is badly short also takes points off every gambit that depends on it, which the game calls strain. Success and failure each have their own story.

howToPlay.heading: Baker Street, and Who Trusts You
howToPlay.body: The five buttons above each scene open one panel at a time. Baker Street gives you Watson's advice (a few times in a game, it shows what each choice will cost), Mycroft's Favour (once, one gauge improves at the cost of another), overheard talk, and Watson's Notebook, his private opinion of the man you are becoming. Company shows how far Watson, Lestrade, Mycroft and Wiggins trust you, and the last thing each was heard to say. Some options open only to a detective they trust, and a few only to one they have lost. Board is your cork board: the traces, people and moves you have pinned up, the Professor's web with the arms you have found and cut (he notices), and the questions you cannot yet answer. Calendar shows where the scene falls in the winter and spring of 1891 and how long to the next date that matters; when your Hours run short it also shows how many days the calendar has already taken from you. Map is the sketch map.

howToPlay.heading: When a Gauge Runs Short
howToPlay.body: A gauge that is badly short makes the others harder: a tired mind reads less, a man without proof is not believed, a discredited man cannot rest. The scene says so while it is true. A man at the bottom is offered a way back, once: a night at Watson's, or a word from Lestrade, if he has earned it. It will not cure a bad road. It will let you keep walking.

howToPlay.heading: Side Cases and Examinations
howToPlay.body: In Act I you may take on one of three small cases, or decline them all and rest. Twice in the story you are asked to examine a scene, three scenes running. Before you leave Baker Street on the last Friday, you may pack a disguise: the priest, the sailor or the clerk. It opens a choice later on that a man in his own face cannot have. Pick what to look at with care: the traces you read decide whether you can state a deduction at the end. A trace you did not read cannot be guessed at.

howToPlay.heading: Four Roads, Chosen Early
howToPlay.body: A few scenes into the story you must choose how to meet the Professor's net: through Scotland Yard, through the street boys of Baker Street, through your brother's club in Whitehall, or by flight across Europe. Each road has its own people and its own endings, and each ends in a short run of scenes that your earlier choices make easier or harder. Some roads are shut until you have earned them.

howToPlay.heading: The Map
howToPlay.body: The map button shows where you are, and the trail you have followed. It is a sketch and not a survey: the streets and the coasts are only approximately where the game puts them.

howToPlay.heading: Look and Sound
howToPlay.body: Settings offers two looks: tweed, a dark parlour with cream paper cards, and paper, the same parlour in daylight. Both have the same houndstooth ground. There are three text sizes, and the atmosphere (a drone of fog and a distant chime) and the sound effects can be turned down or off. Nothing flashes, and motion stops if your device asks for it.

howToPlay.heading: Difficulty
howToPlay.body: On the easiest setting every choice shows its cost first, and a button offers Watson's suggestion for any scene, so that you may read the story with one tap at a time. On the middle setting you must deduce the cost. On the hardest, bribes, tickets and informants cost real money from a thin purse, a choice you cannot afford is shut to you, and a few extra choices are offered only to a man who is short of funds.

howToPlay.heading: What Is Real and What Is Not
howToPlay.body: This game follows the outline of Arthur Conan Doyle's story The Final Problem (1893) and, at the end of one road, The Empty House (1903): Professor Moriarty, the flight across the Continent, the Reichenbach Falls and the return. The four minor cases follow Doyle's A Scandal in Bohemia (1891), The Adventure of the Speckled Band (1892), The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle (1892) and The Adventure of the Red-Headed League (1891). Irene Adler's letter in 1891 is the game's own invention. Most of the scenes, the clerk Larch, Sergeant Pike, the boy Alf and the newspaper clippings are invented. Each ending says, afterwards, what the original story does.

lines: Mrs Hudson: 'There's been a man under the lamp since Tuesday, sir. He isn't selling anything.'
Mrs Hudson: 'Dr Watson called while you were out. He left his card and said you were to eat something.'
A cabman on the rank: 'Fog's thickening, sir. They say it'll be a proper pea-souper by Friday.'
The newsboy: 'Terrible doings in the City, sir! Banks and jewellers and all! Nobody knows who's behind it!'
Mrs Hudson: 'You look a perfect ghost, sir. I never saw such eyes. Do sit down and let me bring you something hot.'
Mrs Hudson: 'I heard you pacing at four this morning. I don't say a word. I only say I heard.'
A constable at the corner: 'Not my business, sir, but they're saying at the station you've been making a nuisance.'
The newsboy: 'They say the Yard doesn't care for you, sir. Not a word of it from me, I'm sure.'
Lestrade, by note: 'Your papers are the talk of the third floor, Mr Holmes. The Chief has asked twice for a meeting.'
Wiggins: 'The boys say the dog-cart's been seen again, Mr Holmes. Black horse, yellow wheels.'
Wiggins: 'There's a man at the corner who reads the same page of the same paper every day. We've named him Mr Slow.'
Mrs Hudson: 'That grey book of yours, sir. I've not touched it. But I never liked the look of it.'
Watson, by note: 'I have had the revolver cleaned. Mary says nothing, but I notice she has begun to sleep lightly.'
A constable: 'Heard the Yard's in a fever, sir. Something about Monday. Nobody will say what.'
The Assistant Commissioner's secretary: 'He has not left his room since breakfast. He has a map.'
Wiggins: 'The boys are tired, Mr Holmes. But they'll go on. They always do.'
A costermonger: 'Funny thing, sir. There's more children out after dark in this street than I've ever known.'
A porter: 'Long way to go, sir, for a gentleman who looks so tired.'
An innkeeper: 'The English are always walking, monsieur. They walk to the water and look at it, and then they walk back.'
Mrs Hudson: 'You're looking a deal better, sir. There's colour in your face. I shall tell the butcher.'
The newsboy: 'There's a gentleman at the Institute says you're a marvel, sir. He's sent a hamper. Mrs Hudson has it in the larder.'
Watson, by note: 'Miss Crewe sends you her kindest regards, and a pot of quince jelly which I'm not at all sure is safe.'
A club servant: 'Nobody talks here, sir, except in the one room. We find that it improves the conversation.'
A Whitehall messenger: 'You'll want the third door, sir, on the left. It's not on the plan, but it's the one they all use.'
A fellow traveller: 'The English, I find, are not so very mad. They are only lonely, and they walk a great deal.'

pos_pos.label: Watson's Holmes
pos_pos.epilogue: In the years that follow, the world remembers a man who kept his friends about him, and who was kinder than he allowed. Those who knew him say that the cold manner was only a coat, worn in public, and that Dr Watson alone was permitted to see what lay beneath.

pos_neutral.label: The Gentleman of Baker Street
pos_neutral.epilogue: He is remembered as a gentleman first and a detective second: courteous to clients, patient with the Yard, tender with the young. It is the kind of reputation that does not make a legend, and makes a great many friends.

pos_neg.label: The Kind Recluse
pos_neg.epilogue: He is remembered as a man who cared a great deal, and said so to nobody. He sent anonymous cheques to the families of the dead, and refused every dinner. The few who guessed the truth said it was the loneliest kindness in London.

neutral_pos.label: The Man With Friends
neutral_pos.epilogue: He is remembered as a man who knew how to work with others: a Doctor, a Brother, an Inspector, a Boy. It was said that he could not do the thing alone, and the saying was true, and he never minded hearing it.

neutral_neutral.label: The Consulting Detective
neutral_neutral.epilogue: He is remembered as the world prefers to remember him: sharp, odd, brilliant and a little aloof. A great reasoner, in the newspapers' phrase, and no more explained than that.

neutral_neg.label: The Solitary
neutral_neg.epilogue: He is remembered as a man who worked alone, because it was easier. The success of his methods was never doubted, and the cost of them was never added up, and in the end it was Mrs Hudson who did the sum.

neg_pos.label: The Brilliant Employer
neg_pos.epilogue: He is remembered as the best mind in London and the most exacting master. He used his friends as he used his microscope, with great skill and little tenderness, and they forgave him for it, because the results were beautiful.

neg_neutral.label: The Calculating Engine
neg_neutral.epilogue: He is remembered as a mind, rather than a man: a machine for solving. Even those who admired him most admitted that they had never quite been sure he would notice if they left the room.

neg_neg.label: The Reasoning Machine
neg_neg.epilogue: He is remembered as a thinking engine with nothing to feed it but the problem. The friends fell away. The clients came and went. In the end the only voice that spoke to him, night after night, was his own.

pos_pos: He has been gentler this month than I have ever known him. He asks after Mary. He eats what he is given. I have begun to suspect that something frightens him very badly.
I think he has decided to need us. It is a great step for a man like Holmes, and I should like to mention that I noticed.
pos_neutral: He is kind, in his sidelong fashion. A shilling to a crossing-sweeper. A word to a nervous client. He would deny every one of them.
He still works alone, but he has begun to leave the door ajar.
pos_neg: He cares for people more than he admits, and will not let them near him. It is the most tiring combination I know.
He has gone off alone again, and written four anonymous cheques. I know his hand, and I know he knows I know.
neutral_pos: He has taken to leaning on us all, I think: myself, Lestrade, even Wiggins. He does not say so. He simply sends for us.
It is a better arrangement than the old one. He is easier to bear, and he has more of his health.
neutral_neutral: He is exactly as he always was. I cannot tell whether that is a comfort or an alarm.
He reads, he plays, he sits. He tells me that he is thinking. I tell him that is what I am afraid of.
neutral_neg: He has drawn the curtains and sent the world away. I find myself loitering on the stairs.
He is a good deal more alone than he was at Christmas, and a good deal less willing to be told so.
neg_pos: He is using us. I do not say that unkindly; we are well used. But I should like to be asked, once, for a reason that is not an errand.
He has become very efficient with other people. I confess I preferred him when he was clumsy.
neg_neutral: There is a hardness in him this month that I do not recall. He speaks of a dead clerk as of a lost paperweight.
I think he is turning into the thing he fights. He is aware of it. I do not think it stops him.
neg_neg: He is cold, and he is alone, and he is very nearly perfect. I find I cannot bear it.
If I did not know him I should say there was nothing in him but the work. Since I know him, I say that there is something still, and it is a long way down.
strand_hours: We are behind, Holmes. I do not say it to scold you. I say it because the Professor keeps a better diary than we do, and he has not wasted a day.
I have counted the days that remain, and I have counted the things that you still wish to do. The two sums do not agree, and I am a doctor, not a conjurer.
Every scene that you read slowly is a day that he spends. I should be very grateful, my dear fellow, for something a little brisk.
strand_hands: You have not a man to spare, Holmes. The boys are tired, Lestrade's constables have other orders, and I am only one doctor. Let us not ask for more than can be sent.
I have looked round the room and counted, and I find that we are fewer than we were. A detective is not one man. You used to say so yourself.
If anyone is to be asked for a favour this week, I should like it to be somebody who has not already given us three.
strand_wires: Nobody has answered a wire of ours in a day and a half. We are working in the dark, Holmes, and the world is a good deal further off than it was.
I have been to the post office twice this morning and have been told nothing at all, very civilly, both times. I do not at all like it.
The newspapers have not telephoned, the clerks have not written, and the street has gone quiet. It is a poor sort of quiet.
strand_plenty: I must say, Holmes, that for once we are very well supplied. The boys, the wires, the hours: I do not think I have seen it so since the Jeremy affair. Do not waste it.
We have men, and time, and a good deal of news coming in. I should like to say that I am confident. I shall say instead that I am watching you very closely.

EASY.label: Watson's Account
EASY.blurb: Every choice shows what it will cost before you commit. For the reader who would sooner follow the story than fight it.

MEDIUM.label: The Consulting Detective
MEDIUM.blurb: No previews. Three calls on Watson's advice. The costs are yours to deduce.

HARD.label: The Empty Purse
HARD.blurb: No previews, and every bribe, ticket and informant is paid for in pounds from a thin purse. Some doors close when the money runs out.

novelNotes.ENDING_CRISIS_EVIDENCE: In the Canon: nothing like this. Doyle's Holmes has always the evidence to hand; the difficulty in The Final Problem is never proof but reach, since the Professor is untouchable by the ordinary law.
novelNotes.ENDING_CRISIS_STANDING: In the Canon: Holmes is sometimes mocked by the police in the early stories, but by 1891 Lestrade and his colleagues generally come to him. A public discrediting is this game's invention.
novelNotes.ENDING_CRISIS_NERVE: In the Canon: Watson often fears for Holmes's health, and records his long fits of languor and his use of cocaine in the earlier stories. A collapse during the Moriarty affair is this game's invention.
novelNotes.ENDING_NET_CLOSES: In the Canon: Moriarty is never tried. In Doyle's story the police take most of his gang on the Monday, but the Professor himself escapes the net and pursues Holmes abroad.
novelNotes.ENDING_NAPOLEON_ESCAPES: In the Canon: this is the story's own turn. The Yard arrests the gang, Moriarty slips away, and Holmes has to leave England. The game lets you play the part that happens off the page.
novelNotes.ENDING_REASON_OF_STATE: In the Canon: there is no such bargain. Doyle's Mycroft is a government man of great reach in later stories, and the closed hearing, the second ledger and the list of names are this game's invention.
novelNotes.ENDING_PRIVATE_WAR: In the Canon: Holmes does not fight a street war against Moriarty. The Baker Street Irregulars, led by Wiggins, are Holmes's street-boy agents in earlier stories, and he pays them a shilling a day.
novelNotes.ENDING_BAKER_STREET_BURNS: In the Canon: Holmes tells Watson that his rooms were set on fire the night before they leave. The attempt fails to kill him. In this game the fire is the Professor's answer to the Shadow War.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_COMPACT: In the Canon: Holmes never takes Moriarty's money. In the story the Professor visits Baker Street to warn him off, and Holmes refuses. The compact is this game's temptation, and its darkest reading of the man.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_FALL: In the Canon: this is Watson's account of The Final Problem. He is decoyed away by a false message about a dying Englishwoman. He returns to find a note, a cigarette-case and a stick, and footprints that go to the edge and not back. Holmes and Moriarty are taken to have fallen together.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_EMPTY_GRAVE: In the Canon: this is the secret told in The Empty House (1903), up to the point where Holmes chooses not to come home. In the story he wrote the note with Moriarty's leave, escaped the Falls, travelled in Tibet, Persia and Khartoum, worked in a laboratory at Montpellier, and returned in 1894; Mycroft alone knew, and supplied him with money. The game lets you stay away.
novelNotes.ENDING_WATSON_STANDS: In the Canon: Watson is not at the Falls. Doyle sent him away, and the whole force of the story falls on the empty path. Watson at Holmes's side is this game's alternative, and the one he deserved.
novelNotes.ENDING_FATAL_SHOT: In the Canon: Colonel Sebastian Moran is Moriarty's chief lieutenant and a celebrated shot. In The Empty House he is the man who fires an air-gun, and Holmes catches him. At the Falls, Doyle gives him no shot at all. Here he fires one.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_RETURN: In the Canon: this is the opening of The Empty House (1903). Holmes returns to London in April 1894, with the Park Lane murder of Ronald Adair as his occasion. He reveals himself to Watson, who faints, and explains afterwards where he has been. The game gives you the choice of how.
novelNotes.ENDING_HER_MAJESTYS_SERVICE: In the Canon: Holmes does work for the Government in later stories, through Mycroft, as in The Bruce-Partington Plans. He is never given a commission, and the game's quiet office off Whitehall is its own invention.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_SECOND_LEDGER: In the Canon: nothing like this. Doyle's Holmes never exposes the powerful to the press, and in Charles Augustus Milverton he burns a blackmailer's letters rather than publish them. The great scandal is this game's invention.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_WOMAN: In the Canon: A Scandal in Bohemia (1891, but set in March 1888). Holmes's one defeat. Irene Adler leaves a letter and her own photograph, and the King offers an emerald ring. Holmes asks for the photograph instead.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_STRONGBOX: Invented. In the story Holmes does not catch Adler; she leaves England with her husband before he can act.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_KING_WAITS: Invented. In the story the King accepts that the matter is closed.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_BAND_RETURNS: In the Canon: The Adventure of the Speckled Band (1892, set in April 1883). Holmes drives the snake back through the ventilator, and Dr Roylott dies of its bite. Holmes says he is indirectly responsible for the death.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_WHISTLE_MISSED: Invented. In the story the case is solved in one night and Helen Stoner lives.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_DOCTOR_LIVES: Invented. In the story Dr Roylott dies of his own snake.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_CHRISTMAS_MERCY: In the Canon: The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle (1892, set at Christmas 1889). Holmes lets Ryder go, saying that it is the season of forgiveness, and that he is 'commuting a felony'.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_STONE_RETURNED: Invented. In the story Holmes does not call the police.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_STONE_LOST: Invented. In the story Ryder is frightened and Holmes lets him go; the stone is recovered.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_LEAGUE_DISSOLVED: In the Canon: The Adventure of the Red-Headed League (1891, set in autumn 1890). Holmes and Peter Jones take John Clay in the cellar of the City and Suburban Bank. In the story it is Holmes who seizes Clay, and Clay's accomplice escapes through the tunnel and is taken by Jones's men at the shop; Holmes says it is all an attempt to escape from the commonplace.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_TUNNEL_OPEN: Invented. In the story the robbery is prevented and the gold is saved.
novelNotes.ENDING_THE_ENCYCLOPAEDIA: Invented. In the story the arrest is public and goes to Scotland Yard; the bank is not kept quiet.
novelNotes.ENDING_CRISIS_STRAND: In the Canon: Holmes is never short of time, helpers or word of the world for long: he has Watson, the Irregulars, Lestrade, his brother and the telegraph. Running out of any of them is this game's invention.

endingHints.ENDING_CRISIS_EVIDENCE: Let the case run dry: choose the options that cost Evidence until nothing remains.
endingHints.ENDING_CRISIS_STANDING: Quarrel with the Yard and break the law until nobody will listen.
endingHints.ENDING_CRISIS_NERVE: Work without rest until the mind refuses.
endingHints.ENDING_NET_CLOSES: Go to the Yard with a strong case and spring the trap at the right door.
endingHints.ENDING_NAPOLEON_ESCAPES: Close the file too soon, fail a finale, or walk out of a room, and let the Professor go.
endingHints.ENDING_REASON_OF_STATE: Accept your brother's arrangement in the Yard route.
endingHints.ENDING_PRIVATE_WAR: Take the street road, and break the Professor with everything you have.
endingHints.ENDING_BAKER_STREET_BURNS: Lose the fight at the Limehouse wharf.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_COMPACT: Listen to the Professor's offer on the first day, and return to it at the end.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_FALL: Go to the Falls, and lose the struggle on the path, or hold the Professor and go over with him.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_EMPTY_GRAVE: Survive the Falls, spend the years away, and choose in 1894 not to come home.
endingHints.ENDING_WATSON_STANDS: Take Watson into your confidence early, and keep him beside you at the Falls.
endingHints.ENDING_FATAL_SHOT: Meet Colonel Moran on the ridge and lose the climb or the gunfight.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_RETURN: Survive the Falls, win the struggle, and choose to come home from the years away.
endingHints.ENDING_HER_MAJESTYS_SERVICE: Take the road through your brother's club, and accept the Government's terms in full.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_SECOND_LEDGER: Take the road through your brother's club, read the second ledger, and put it in the newspapers.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_WOMAN: In Bohemia, accept that you have been beaten and take her portrait.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_STRONGBOX: In Bohemia, follow her abroad and win the photograph back.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_KING_WAITS: In Bohemia, tell the King what he wants to hear, and nothing more.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_BAND_RETURNS: At Stoke Moran, drive the snake back before it reaches the bed.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_WHISTLE_MISSED: At Stoke Moran, be slow with the cane, or warn the Doctor you are coming.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_DOCTOR_LIVES: At Stoke Moran, leave the snake to the constables, or break the door too late.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_CHRISTMAS_MERCY: In the Carbuncle case, let James Ryder go on Christmas night.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_STONE_RETURNED: In the Carbuncle case, send for Lestrade.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_STONE_LOST: In the Carbuncle case, press Ryder for a confession and let him run.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_LEAGUE_DISSOLVED: In the Red-Headed League, take Clay in the cellar, or let the Yard do it.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_TUNNEL_OPEN: In the Red-Headed League, be a half-second late, or go home to bed.
endingHints.ENDING_THE_ENCYCLOPAEDIA: In the Red-Headed League, take Clay quietly and keep the bank's name out of the papers.
endingHints.ENDING_CRISIS_STRAND: Spend your Hours, your Hands or your Wires down to nothing: work slowly, work alone, or cut yourself off.

flagNotes.noticed: The Professor learned your face early, when your visit to his house went badly.
flagNotes.irregulars: You hired Wiggins and the Baker Street Irregulars.
flagNotes.larchTalks: Tobias Larch lived long enough to give his statement.
flagNotes.larchLost: Tobias Larch died before he could testify.
flagNotes.ledger: You held the Professor's grey ledger.
flagNotes.breakIn: You broke into the Professor's coaching house.
flagNotes.watsonIn: You took Watson into your confidence.
flagNotes.watsonSpared: You kept Watson out of it, and told him a lie.
flagNotes.heardOffer: You listened to the Professor's offer.
flagNotes.warrantsSworn: The warrants for Monday's raids were properly sworn.
flagNotes.mycroftOwed: You owe Mycroft a favour for the Home Office minute.

flagNotes.moleUsed: You turned the leak at the Yard into a trap.
flagNotes.moranSeen: You met Colonel Moran's air-gun in the dark.
flagNotes.houseTaken: You seized the Professor's own house.
flagNotes.directed: You ran the eleven raids from the Yard's telegraph.
flagNotes.stateBargain: You accepted a closed hearing for the Professor.
flagNotes.mycroftTold: Mycroft told you what the Government feared.
flagNotes.vigilante: You worked outside the law, and the Yard noticed.
flagNotes.boySent: You sent a child into the Anchor and Hope.
flagNotes.routeKnown: You learned the road the Professor's carriage takes.
flagNotes.moranMarked: You saw Colonel Moran's face by lamplight.
flagNotes.hudsonSafe: You sent Mrs Hudson to Brighton before the fire.
flagNotes.promisedLestrade: You promised Lestrade to stay within the law.
flagNotes.bankRun: You froze the Professor's money in Lombard Street.
flagNotes.rivalry: You set the Professor's lieutenants against one another.
flagNotes.followed: You followed the arsonist to a house with a green door.
flagNotes.priest: You left London dressed as an Italian priest.
flagNotes.mycroftFunds: Mycroft's money followed you across the Continent.
flagNotes.lettersWritten: You wrote the whole story down at Meiringen.
flagNotes.watsonStays: Watson stayed at your side on the path.
flagNotes.watsonDecoyed: Watson was sent to an empty hotel.
flagNotes.watsonSent: Watson was sent to Interlaken with a letter.
flagNotes.noteLeft: You left a note for Watson on the rock.
flagNotes.mycroftFavour: You called in a favour from Mycroft.
flagNotes.clueHeel: You read the heel-print on the roof in Vere Street.
flagNotes.clueCab: You followed the cab's ruts to the mews gate.
flagNotes.fitchNamed: You named the cabman Fitch from the Kentish Town yard.
flagNotes.yardLearned: You learned what the Kentish Town yard is for.
flagNotes.governessSafe: You kept Miss Crewe out of the Professor's hands.
flagNotes.governessBait: You used Miss Crewe as bait for the printer.
flagNotes.dogcart: The boys found the dog-cart with the yellow wheels.
flagNotes.confessed: You owned up to the break-in at Marylebone.
flagNotes.pressInformed: You gave the Standard its exclusive for Monday night.
flagNotes.secretaryTalks: The bishop's secretary told you the cab-yards.
flagNotes.pawnbrokerTalks: Mrs Venn gave you the key to the cipher.
flagNotes.clueDoor: You found the panel behind the Professor's desk.
flagNotes.clueGuide: You learned the missing book was a railway guide.
flagNotes.studyRead: You read where the Professor went from his study.
flagNotes.watchSet: Your watch on the house in Hackney was properly set.
flagNotes.roofWatch: Wiggins's boys held the rooftops in Hackney.
flagNotes.canalOnly: You staked the whole watch on the canal.
flagNotes.printerTurns: The printer sailed for Canada and left you his plates.
flagNotes.boysStand: The boys stayed, because you told them the truth.
flagNotes.boysFewer: Five of the boys went home, and seven stayed.
flagNotes.byWater: You came to the wharf by water.
flagNotes.byRoof: You came to the wharf over the roof.
flagNotes.openQuay: You walked down the quay in the open.
flagNotes.moranDown: You put the Colonel out of the fight.
flagNotes.strangerShaken: You shook the stranger on the Basel train.
flagNotes.watsonWarned: You told Watson what you meant to do at the Falls.
flagNotes.ledgeKnown: You walked the ledge above the Falls with Hans.
flagNotes.tellNoOne: You told no one that you lived.
flagNotes.mycroftKnows: You told your brother, and him alone, that you lived.
flagNotes.wroteWatson: Your letter from Florence reached Watson.
flagNotes.moranKnows: Your letter from Florence was opened by the wrong man.
flagNotes.returnedEarly: You came home once in 1893 to sit with Watson.
flagNotes.dramaticReturn: You returned as an old bookseller.
flagNotes.gentleReturn: You returned by the old stair, to a supper laid.
flagNotes.lawClause: You wrote the law into the Government's terms.
flagNotes.homeOfficeWarrant: You carried the Home Secretary's warrant.
flagNotes.readSecond: You read the second ledger to the last page.
flagNotes.cleanHands: You would not open the second ledger.
flagNotes.specialBranch: Special Branch took the Professor's house in silence.
flagNotes.ministerTurned: Lord Harcastle talked, and was spared.
flagNotes.ministerHeld: You hold Lord Harcastle's word in your pocket-book.
flagNotes.immunityAccepted: You backed your brother's immunity for the Professor.
flagNotes.bohemiaFull: The King told you the whole of it, letters included.
flagNotes.bohemiaKnown: You told the King that you knew who he was.
flagNotes.bohemiaTerms: You took the King's thousand pounds on your own terms.
flagNotes.bohemiaGroom: You played an out-of-work groom in the mews at Briony Lodge.
flagNotes.bohemiaWatch: You watched Briony Lodge from across the road.
flagNotes.bohemiaWatson: Watson waited at the corner with the smoke-rocket.
flagNotes.bohemiaPhoto: You saw where she hides the photograph: the panel behind the bell-pull.
flagNotes.bohemiaSuspect: She saw through the ruse at once.
flagNotes.bohemiaBurglar: You searched her house at night and left a card.
flagNotes.bohemiaWaited: You waited in the street, and she left in the night.
flagNotes.bandNoon: You promised Miss Stoner that you would come by noon.
flagNotes.bandLondon: You learned what the money is and when it is due.
flagNotes.bandSurgeon: The police surgeon has seen Miss Stoner.
flagNotes.bandRope: The bell-rope is a dummy, and the ventilator opens into the Doctor's room.
flagNotes.bandMilk: A saucer of milk on the safe, and a dog-lash with a loop.
flagNotes.bandBend: Dr Roylott came home early and bent the poker.
flagNotes.bandAnimals: A cheetah, a baboon and a camp of gipsies keep the house.
flagNotes.bandVigil: You waited in the dark with a cane.
flagNotes.bandWatson: Watson waited at the window with his revolver.
flagNotes.bandWarned: You warned Dr Roylott that you were watching him.
flagNotes.carbAdvert: You advertised for Henry Baker in four evening papers.
flagNotes.carbStone: You tested the stone against a pane of glass.
flagNotes.carbClub: You learned of the goose-club at the Alpha Inn.
flagNotes.carbTruth: You told Henry Baker what was in his goose.
flagNotes.carbQuiet: You said nothing to Henry Baker about the stone.
flagNotes.carbOakshott: Mrs Oakshott of Brixton Road reared the geese.
flagNotes.carbPaid: You paid for the name of Mrs Oakshott.
flagNotes.carbFollow: You followed the ferret-faced man and found James Ryder.
flagNotes.leagueFull: Jabez Wilson told you the whole of the story.
flagNotes.leagueAssistant: The assistant works for half wages, and spends an hour at a time in the cellar.
flagNotes.leagueCard: You held the card from the office door to the light.
flagNotes.leagueKnees: The assistant's trousers are worn through at the knee.
flagNotes.leagueBank: The pawnbroker's cellar backs on to the City and Suburban Bank.
flagNotes.leagueVault: Mr Merryweather lent you the vault key.
flagNotes.leagueMen: Mr Jones brought four men and handcuffs.
flagNotes.leagueAlone: You said that you would wait in the cellar alone.
flagNotes.leanYard: You took it to Scotland Yard first.
flagNotes.leanStreet: You sent for the boys first.
flagNotes.leanMycroft: You went to your brother's club first.
flagNotes.leanFlight: You trusted no one, and kept the road out of England open.
flagNotes.greavesKnown: Mycroft introduced you to Superintendent Greaves.
flagNotes.priceNamed: Mycroft told you what Whitehall would cost.
flagNotes.fofClerk: You followed the Foreign Office clerk to Kensington.
flagNotes.routePlanned: You planned your road out of England in February.
flagNotes.restTaken: You took a night's rest, and mended.
flagNotes.standingRepaired: Lestrade vouched for you, and it cost him.
flagNotes.dsSailor: You packed the old sailor's jacket and beard.
flagNotes.dsClerk: You packed the clerk's coat and bowler.
flagNotes.adlerMet: Mrs Norton, once Irene Adler, wrote to you, and you called.
flagNotes.buyerNamed: Mr Hector Dunmore of Brandt and Chambers is buying for the Professor.
flagNotes.adlerBait: You asked Mrs Norton to sell, and followed the money.
flagNotes.adlerAbroad: Mrs Norton went abroad, with the packet.
flagNotes.clueBook: The Professor's cipher is made of groups of four figures, none above four hundred: a book.
flagNotes.clueTitle: Every cable opens with the same five groups: a title.
flagNotes.cipherBroken: You read the Professor's cipher: his own treatise, by page and line.
flagNotes.knowsDeparture: The Professor means to sail from Southampton on Tuesday.
flagNotes.mycroftAlone: You would not sit in the room with the Professor, and Mycroft bore it alone.
flagNotes.wharfTide: The Teal comes up on the top of the tide on Tuesday, a quarter past eight, and never takes a load.
flagNotes.wharfWatch: A tall, stooping man went into the wharf on Sunday and did not come out.
flagNotes.wharfPolice: The wharf is leased in the name of Mr Alexander Bell, who does not exist.
flagNotes.wharfMarks: Three crosses and a bar, chalked on every bollard: a route to the cellar stair.
flagNotes.wharfOil: Forty-one casks of lamp-oil at the wharf gate, and the tops are off.
flagNotes.wharfCarter: You followed the carter who brings the bread.
flagNotes.registerRead: There is no sick English lady at the Englischer Hof.
flagNotes.guideTalks: Every guide in Meiringen has been paid to be somewhere else.
flagNotes.formsRead: The message that will call Watson away is in a man's hand, on a post-office form.
flagNotes.pathRead: You walked the path above the Falls and read the ground.
flagNotes.cleftSeen: There is a cleft in the rock below the ledge, big enough for one man lying flat.
flagNotes.adlerWarned: Mrs Norton warned you of a forged message for Watson.
flagNotes.adlerWatch: Mrs Norton is watching the hotel for you.
flagNotes.adlerSent: You sent Mrs Norton back to Brussels.
flagNotes.adlerStatement: Mrs Norton gave a sworn statement to Lestrade.
flagNotes.adlerSafe: You told Mrs Norton to stay out of court and out of London.
flagNotes.adlerDecoy: Mrs Norton dined with Mr Dunmore at the Café Royal and learned the door and the hour.
flagNotes.adlerHurt: Mr Dunmore saw through Mrs Norton at the Café Royal.
